title: Episode 34: The Johnson County War: Cattle Barons and the Invaders
description:
In April 1892, northern Wyoming became the battlefield for the most infamous range war in American history: the Johnson County War. Wealthy cattle barons of the Wyoming Stock Growers Association hired twenty-four Texas mercenaries, chartered a private train from Cheyenne, and invaded Johnson County with a hit list of seventy small ranchers, leading to a heroic last stand at the KC Cabin and a three-day siege at the TA Ranch.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In the late nineteenth century, the open grasslands of Wyoming were ruled by an elite, all-powerful oligarchy of aristocratic cattle barons known as the Wyoming Stock Growers Association. Headquartered in the opulent Cheyenne Club, where wealthy British lords and Harvard graduates drank vintage French wine and traded cattle herds, the association controlled the state government, the governor, and the courts. But when small homesteaders and independent ranchers arrived under the Homestead Act to fence off land, the cattle barons branded them all as thieves and rustlers. In the spring of eighteen ninety-two, the association launched an audacious, illegal military invasion: chartering a secret private train, hiring twenty-four Texas gunfighters, and riding north with a death list of seventy men. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE CHEYENNE CLUB OLIGARCHY
In the eighteen eighties, the Wyoming Territory was not a democratic society; it was a feudal cattle kingdom. Sprawling across millions of acres of unfenced public grasslands were massive corporate cattle syndicates, owned by prominent territorial politicians, Wall Street investment houses, and wealthy English and Scottish aristocrats. The nerve center of this livestock empire was the legendary Cheyenne Club. Located in the territorial capital of Cheyenne, the club was an enclave of unimaginable Victorian opulence: it featured imported Persian rugs, walnut-paneled billiard rooms, private French chefs, and cellars stocked with vintage champagne and fine Havana cigars. Within these private dining rooms, members of the Wyoming Stock Growers Association dictated the rangeland laws of the territory. Under association-crafted statutes, any unbranded stray calf found on the open range was legally deemed the exclusive property of the association, and independent roundups were treated as grand larceny. But following the catastrophic winter blizzard of eighteen eighty-six and eighty-seven—the infamous 'Great Die-Up,' which killed eighty percent of open-range cattle and devastated the barons' speculative empires—a wave of independent homesteaders, former cowboys, and small farming families poured into northern Wyoming's Johnson County. These small settlers built barbed-wire fences around their quarter-sections, filed legal land claims under the Homestead Act, and flatly refused to submit to the Cheyenne Club's corporate monopoly. In the grand parlor of the Cheyenne Club, the cattle barons regarded the vast open ranges of Wyoming as their private feudal estates, considering any independent homesteader who fenced a waterhole to be a criminal usurper.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE LYNCHINGS AND THE RED NECKTIES
Determined to protect their dominance over the public grazing lands, the cattle barons launched a campaign of intimidation and terror. They branded every independent homesteader as a 'rustler' and used friendly newspapers in Cheyenne to whip up public hysteria. In July eighteen eighty-nine, association sympathizers abducted a popular female homesteader named Ellen Watson—falsely slandered in the press as 'Cattle Kate'—and her partner Jim Averell, hanging both of them from a cottonwood tree along the Sweetwater River without a trial. No one was ever punished for the lynching, as key witnesses mysteriously vanished. By eighteen ninety-one, small ranchers in Johnson County had had enough. Led by charismatic local cowboy Nate Champion, the small cattlemen formed their own independent livestock association, announcing that they would hold their own spring roundup on the public ranges in defiance of the Cheyenne Club. To show their solidarity, the homesteaders wore red bandanas around their necks, defiantly calling themselves the 'Red Necks.' Furious that small homesteaders dared to challenge their authority, the cattle barons decided that legal harassment was no longer sufficient: they would physically eradicate the leadership of Johnson County. The homesteaders recognized that their very survival depended upon unity. By organizing their own spring roundup, the small ranchers directly challenged the economic monopoly that had choked the territory for a generation.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE SECRET DEATH TRAIN
In March eighteen ninety-two, leaders of the Stock Growers Association—including prominent cattleman Frank Wolcott and former territorial governor George Baxter—met in secret in Cheyenne. With the tacit blessing of sitting Wyoming Governor Amos Barber and United States Senators Francis E. Warren and Joseph M. Carey, the barons organized a private mercenary army. Acting through an agent in Texas, they recruited twenty-four seasoned Texas gunslingers, paying them five dollars a day plus a bonus of fifty dollars for every homesteader they killed. On the night of April fifth, eighteen ninety-two, a special chartered six-car train pulled into the Union Pacific rail yard in Cheyenne. The train was loaded with three flatcars carrying forty prime horses, supply wagons, thousands of rounds of ammunition, and a luxury Pullman sleeper car carrying fifty-two heavily armed men: the twenty-four Texas mercenaries, alongside twenty wealthy Wyoming cattle barons, two medical doctors, and a hand-picked reporter from the Chicago Tribune. In their coat pockets was a typed hit list containing seventy names, with Nate Champion and Johnson County Sheriff Red Angus at the very top. The train slipped out of Cheyenne under cover of total darkness, heading north toward Casper. The mercenaries were outfitted with brand-new Winchester repeating rifles, English hunting coats, and cases of ammunition paid for by corporate bank accounts in New York and London.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE LAST STAND OF NATE CHAMPION
Unloading in Casper before dawn, the mercenary army—now calling themselves 'The Invaders'—mounted their horses and rode north through freezing sleet toward the Johnson County seat of Buffalo. On the morning of April ninth, eighteen ninety-two, the Invaders surrounded the KC Cabin on the Powder River, where Nate Champion and three companions were staying. They captured two trappers stepping outside for water, then fatally shot homesteader Nick Ray as he walked out the door. Nate Champion dragged his dying friend back inside and barricaded the door. For the next nine hours, Nate Champion staged one of the most heroic solitary defenses in Western history. Armed with a Winchester rifle, Champion fired from windows and rifle slits, holding all fifty-two Invaders at bay and wounding three gunmen. In between gun battles, Champion sat at the cabin table and calmly wrote in his pocket diary, recording the progress of the siege: 'Boys, I feel pretty lonesome just now. I wish there was someone here with me so we could talk, but I will do the best I can on my own.' At four in the afternoon, the Invaders pushed a wagon loaded with burning hay against the rear wall, setting the wooden cabin ablaze. Choking on thick black smoke, Champion leaped from the burning building with his six-shooter blazing, sprinting for the creek ravine before being cut down by a volley of twenty-eight bullets. Champion final diary entry, found bloodstained in his coat pocket beside his riddled body, was published in newspapers across the country, transforming the lone cowboy into an immortal martyr of the American homestead.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE SIEGE OF THE TA RANCH
The Invaders believed Champion's death would terrify the settlers into submission, but it had the exact opposite effect. A passing neighbor who witnessed the attack galloped seventy miles north into Buffalo, shouting the alarm: 'The Invaders are coming! Nate Champion has been murdered!' An electrifying wave of fury swept through Johnson County. County Sheriff William 'Red' Angus mobilized a massive citizens' posse: over four hundred armed homesteaders, cowboys, town merchants, and farmers grabbed their rifles, mounted horses, and rode south to intercept the mercenaries. Realizing they were vastly outnumbered by an enraged populace, the Invaders panicked and retreated into the fortified log barns and ranch house of the TA Ranch on Crazy Woman Creek. The homesteaders encircled the ranch, digging trenches and building a rolling wooden assault barricade called a 'Go-Devil.' For three days, the settlers laid siege to the TA Ranch, firing thousands of rounds into the log buildings and preparing to blast the barricades with dynamite. Frank Wolcott and the trapped cattle barons realized they were hours away from being wiped out to the last man. Settlers rode through the night from across three counties to join Sheriff Angus, determined that the corporate invaders would not escape justice for the cold-blooded murders at the KC Cabin.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: RESCUE BY THE CAVALRY
Facing imminent annihilation, an Invader managed to slip through the lines at night and reach a telegraph depot. In Cheyenne, Governor Barber immediately telegraphed President Benjamin Harrison in Washington, claiming that an 'insurrection' was taking place in Wyoming and begging for federal military intervention. In the predawn hours of April thirteenth, eighteen ninety-two, Colonel J.J. Van Horn marched three troops of the Ninth United States Cavalry from nearby Fort McKinney, galloping between the trenches just as the homesteaders were lighting dynamite fuses. The cattle barons and their Texas mercenaries eagerly surrendered to the federal soldiers to escape the wrath of the settlers' posse. Although the Invaders were transported under guard to Cheyenne for trial, the cattle barons used their immense political influence to corrupt the legal process. The defense successfully delayed proceedings until Johnson County was bankrupted by court costs, and in January eighteen ninety-three, all charges against the Invaders were quietly dismissed.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE LEGACY OF THE HOMESTEADER TRIUMPH
Yet while the cattle barons escaped criminal punishment behind the closed doors of Cheyenne courtrooms, their absolute political and economic hegemony over Wyoming was permanently broken. In the state elections of eighteen ninety-two, outraged Wyoming homesteaders and working-class citizens organized at the ballot box, sweeping the pro-baron Republican politicians out of power in a historic landslide. The Wyoming Stock Growers Association was forced to open its membership to small ranchers, and independent cattle roundups were legally protected. The heroic sacrifice of Nate Champion became immortalized across the West, inspiring countless songs, books, and films, including Michael Cimino's epic cinematic masterpiece Heaven's Gate. Today, the rolling pastures of Johnson County remain dotted with family-owned ranches rather than corporate feudal estates—an enduring monument to the courage of everyday settlers who stood their ground against armed oligarchs and proved that the promise of the American frontier belonged to all who worked the soil.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Johnson County War is an unforgettable chapter in American frontier history, revealing the raw struggle between entrenched corporate oligarchy and independent homesteaders. It proves that the true spirit of the American West belonged not to the cattle barons in their luxury clubs, but to the everyday settlers who stood firm on their land. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next Tuesday as we continue our journey across the American saga. Until then, stay curious.
